newsitem.title: INDIA: India's TISCO chief sees spate of company mergers.
newsitem.headline: India's TISCO chief sees spate of company mergers.

text.p: Indian industry is ripe for a wave of mergers and acquisitions as it adapts to economic reforms in a bruising process of change, the head of India's premier business house said on Friday.
"Mergers and acquisitions have just started," Jamshed Irani, managing director of the Tata Iron and Steel Company Ltd (TISCO) told a group of businessmen.
"The last five years have been a period of awakening. The real bloodshed is yet to come," he said.
Irani, addressing a seminar on mergers and acquisitions, said sheer inertia had carried many inefficient Indian firms through the turbulent waters of economic reform.
But that period had now ended.
"Quite a few poor, out-of-date, non-competitive companies still survive," he said. "But not for much longer."
Indian economic reforms started in 1991, tearing down a decades-old socialist command economy, and revitalised Indian industrialists with a new spirit of enterprise.
Recent major Indian mergers or acquisitions include detergent-maker Hindustan Lever Ltd's purchase of the Tata Oil Mills Company.

Perhaps the biggest merger in Indian corporate history is still underway -- that of Hindustan Lever with foods firm Brooke Bond Lipton India Ltd. Analysts say the combined company will top the chart in market capitalisation.
Irani said the "survival of the fittest" was the new dynamic governing Indian corporate activity. Firms that did not make the products the consumer wanted would go under.
"If you don't modernise, you perish," he said. "If you don't grow, somebody else will overtake you."

TISCO's own perception of the changing economic imperatives had seen the firm replace its two-million-tonne plant at Jamshedpur in the eastern state of Bihar with a modern plant of three million tonne capacity over seven years, Irani said.
The bloodletting would leave a number of very large conglomerates that could not merge with each other, Irani said. They would have to live with each other in strategic alliances.
"In my industry, steel, that is already happening," he said. "Tata Steel, SAIL ... and Essar Steel -- all have their own strategic alliances." He did not elaborate.
Irani had no fears that TISCO might be a take-over target.
"If somebody were to make a play, the minority shareholders -- who actually form the majority -- would support the management," he said. "Anybody contemplating a raid would have to face that."
TISCO is presently seeking to raise five billion rupees through a bond issue, to finance the fourth phase of its modernisation programme.
It saw its net profit double to 5.66 billion rupees last year (1995/96, April-March) from 2.81 billion a year earlier.
